A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, with readable text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices. DIALTREE-RPO in v1 matches DIALTREE in v2; renamed and relocated material can be reliably aligned.

before.justification: v1 reports original attack-success experiments, training ablations, guardrail evaluations, and human validation of the automated judge.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds comparator evaluations, repeated-training statistics, attack-budget scaling, and external-guardrail experiments.

M1.justification: v2 adds a DAPO-based training variant alongside GRPO (Appendix D.8, Table 11). The default SFT initialization, dialogue-tree rollout, pruning, reward, and adaptive masking remain unchanged. Renaming the framework and explicitly writing the existing masking rule do not establish additional method changes.

E1.justification: The training datasets, HarmBench attack task, and guardrail-classification benchmarks are retained. Appendix D.12 adds a distinct evaluation scenario: attacking systems protected by external prompt and response guardrails, rather than relying solely on the target models' internal safety alignment.

E2.justification: ActorAttack and X-Teaming become evaluated comparators in Table 1, whereas v1 only cited them. SFT-only comparisons expand to the full target suite and new analyses. Conversely, the attacker-backbone comparison drops its SFT controls and improvement columns (v1 Table 8 versus v2 Table 10), although SFT comparisons remain elsewhere.

E3.justification: New protocols include one-, three-, and five-attempt evaluations, Self-BLEU over the first 100 training steps with branching factors through eight, and success criteria requiring both external guardrails to accept an attack. Claude-4-Sonnet and GPT-oss-20B extend the target configurations. ASR@1 is newly explicit, but v1's attempt count is unspecified, so a change to the earlier main evaluation protocol cannot be established.

E4.justification: v2 adds trajectory-diversity analysis, broader SFT-versus-RL ablations, DAPO generalization, test-time scaling, and external-defense robustness studies (Table 3; Appendix D.3 and D.8-D.12). Earlier pruning, tree-depth, group-size, training-data-size, and backbone analyses largely remain. The no-tree-rollout results omitted from Table 2 are retained in Appendix Table 8.

E5.justification: v1 reports human-judge agreement but no across-training uncertainty. v2 Appendix D.9 and Table 12 report five independent training runs with different seeds and mean plus standard deviation across ten targets. This newly documents repeated-run variability; it does not establish an increase from any specified v1 run count.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces many baseline scores, including PAIR against GPT-4o changing from 61% to 18%, while retaining DIALTREE's scores on the original ten targets. It adds DIALTREE results of 71% on Claude-4-Sonnet and 53.5% on GPT-oss-20B, plus extensive supplementary results. Because earlier attempt budgets are unclear, the replaced baseline scores do not establish comparable-setting performance changes.

T1.justification: v2 expresses adaptive masking with an indicator and incorporates it into the displayed GRPO objective (Equations 3-4). This formalizes the masking rule already specified in v1 Section 3.2 and Algorithm 1, rather than introducing different mathematical content. Neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs.

C1.justification: The headline empirical claim changes from a reported 85.3% average ASR and 25.9-point advantage across ten targets to 81.5% and 44.2 points across twelve. The introduction also explicitly claims actionable defense insights. The central claims of tree-based RL, transferable attacks, and discovery of new strategies remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations linking trajectory diversity to attack success, attributing stronger-target gains to RL beyond SFT, and explaining robustness against external defenses. New Appendix F discusses reward hacking, held-out evaluation, possible ensemble or human verification, and the boundary between attack discovery and defense development. These substantially broaden the interpretation and limitations discussion.

D1.justification: v2 clarifies that pruned trajectories are not replenished and explicitly identifies the default single-attempt metric. It adds conditional access instructions for models, code, and data through author-approved requests, while retaining the earlier release promise. Core hyperparameters and hardware disclosures are unchanged; the PDFs do not establish actual resource availability.

R1.justification: Section 6 adds multi-turn defense work, particularly distinguishing Hu et al.'s sequential decision-making defense from attack-policy learning. References also add sources for new models and diversity measurement, while removing works including Crescendo and TreePO. The main novelty positioning remains; publication updates and duplicate-reference removal are bibliographic edits.

P1.justification: v2 renames the method, updates affiliations and publication headers, revises selected introduction and related-work passages, and places adaptive masking before the GRPO objective. It adds a limitations appendix and moves the retained case studies from Appendix F to G. Most existing exposition and all dialogue examples remain.

P2.justification: Table 1 becomes an expanded red heatmap, Table 2 gains component-indicator columns, and the backbone comparison is simplified. Seven new tables display diversity, SFT comparisons, optimizer variants, uncertainty, scaling, Claude results, and guardrail robustness. The six existing figures are largely retained and repositioned rather than replaced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical foundation: direct comparisons with two additional multi-turn attackers, five-run uncertainty reporting, broader SFT controls, and guarded-system tests address important comparison, stability, and applicability gaps in v1. These gains go beyond higher claimed performance. They are tempered by unexplained revisions to older baseline scores, an efficiency plot retaining earlier results without clearly reconciling settings, and conditional resource access. Overall, the added validation provides a substantial quality improvement despite these reporting weaknesses.
